body:
Meaning and purpose of GIS

A Geographical Information System (GIS) is a computer-based system used to collect, store, manage, analyse and display information associated with geographical locations.

A conventional map shows the geographical distribution of selected features. GIS can additionally connect those features with descriptive information, combine multiple datasets, examine spatial relationships and generate new maps from the results.

GIS is a system for managing and analysing geographically referenced information. Its distinctive function is to connect information about geographical features with their locations.

Components of GIS

  • Hardware: Computers, storage devices and associated equipment.
  • Software: Programs for processing, analysing and displaying geographical information.
  • Data: Maps, imagery, coordinates and descriptive records.
  • People: Individuals who collect, manage, interpret and use geographical information.
  • Methods: Procedures followed to ensure reliable data management and analysis.

Spatial data and attribute data

Spatial data describes the location, shape and geographical extent of features. It answers questions such as where a river flows, where a village is situated and what area a forest occupies.

Attribute data describes the properties of geographical features. It may include names, population, land use, road type, soil category or other characteristics.

For a village, its geographical coordinates and boundary constitute spatial information, whereas its name and population constitute attribute information. GIS connects these 2 forms of data.

Thematic layers

GIS commonly organises geographical information into separate thematic layers. Each layer represents a particular category of information for a geographical area.

A district-level GIS may contain separate layers for rivers, roads, village boundaries, elevation, soil, vegetation and rainfall. These layers can be viewed individually or combined to study relationships between different features.

Layers do not have to originate from the same source. Satellite imagery may provide vegetation information, field observations may supply geographical coordinates and census records may supply village population data.

Georeferencing and coordinate systems

Georeferencing associates an image, map or other dataset with known geographical positions so that its features can be placed correctly in relation to other datasets.

Geographical coordinates, commonly expressed as latitude and longitude, identify positions on the Earth. Projected coordinate systems represent positions on a flat mapping surface and can support appropriate distance and area measurements.

Datasets using different coordinate systems may need to be transformed before they can be analysed together. If datasets are incorrectly positioned, roads, rivers or boundaries representing the same area may fail to align.

Raster and vector data

Raster data

Raster data represents geographical space as a regular grid of cells or pixels. Each cell contains a value describing a geographical property.

Satellite images, elevation grids and many continuous geographical surfaces are commonly represented in raster format. Raster data can also represent categories such as land-cover classes.

Vector data

Vector data represents geographical features through coordinates using points, lines and polygons.

  • Point: Represents a geographical location, such as a well or school.
  • Line: Represents a linear feature, such as a road or river.
  • Polygon: Represents an enclosed area, such as a district, lake or agricultural field.

The choice of representation depends partly on map scale and purpose. A city may be represented as a point on a national map but as a polygon on a detailed urban map.

Data quality and metadata

Geographical datasets differ in accuracy, resolution, observation date and completeness. A reliable GIS analysis requires attention to these differences.

Metadata is information describing a dataset. It may specify its source, date of collection, coordinate system, resolution, accuracy and methods of preparation. Metadata helps users decide whether a dataset is suitable for a particular geographical analysis.

Prelims focus

  • GIS links geographical location with descriptive information.
  • Spatial data describes location and geometry; attribute data describes properties.
  • Thematic layers represent separate categories of geographical information.
  • Raster data uses cells or pixels; vector data uses points, lines and polygons.
  • Georeferencing assigns geographical positions to datasets.
  • Trap: Raster data is not limited to photographs, and vector data is not limited to points.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Practical Work in Geography, Part II, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 4, Spatial Information Technology, pp. 46–56; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Class 11, Geography, 2020 reprint, Chapter 16, Geographical Information and Map Making, pp. 121–122; US Geological Survey, What Is a Geographic Information System (GIS)?; National Remote Sensing Centre, Quick Reference Guide on GIS, data models and spatial data sections. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Geographical Information Systems: Components, Data and Layers

body:
Meaning of spatial analysis

Spatial analysis is the examination of geographical locations, distributions and relationships to obtain information that is not immediately evident from individual datasets.

GIS allows users to answer questions about proximity, connectivity, geographical overlap, terrain and the distribution of resources.

Attribute and spatial queries

An attribute query selects features according to their recorded properties. For example, a GIS can select villages with populations greater than 5,000 using their population records.

A spatial query selects features according to geographical relationships. For example, a GIS can identify villages situated within a flood-affected area or schools located near a particular road.

Both types of query can be combined to identify villages with populations greater than 5,000 that also lie within a flood-affected zone.

Overlay analysis

Overlay analysis combines geographical layers covering the same area to examine their relationships or produce a new dataset.

For example, a flood extent layer can be overlaid with village boundaries and agricultural land layers to identify affected villages and cropland.

Two elementary overlay operations are:

  • Intersection: Retains areas common to the input layers.
  • Union: Retains the combined geographical extent of the input polygon layers, including their overlapping and non-overlapping areas.

Overlay analysis is particularly useful for identifying locations that satisfy several geographical conditions simultaneously.

Buffer analysis

A buffer is an area created around a geographical feature at a specified distance.

For example, a 500 m buffer around a river identifies land within 500 m of the mapped river feature, while a 2 km buffer around a school identifies locations within that distance of the school.

Buffers may be created around point, line or polygon features. They are useful in proximity analysis, environmental planning and identifying areas potentially affected by geographical phenomena.

An ordinary distance buffer does not automatically represent actual travel distance, travel time or a scientifically established hazard boundary. A location within a river buffer is not necessarily flood-prone, because flooding also depends on elevation, drainage and other conditions.

Network analysis

Network analysis studies interconnected geographical features such as roads, railways and transport networks. It can be used to identify suitable routes, estimate travel distances and examine accessibility.

A school may be only 1 km from a settlement in a straight line but require a 3 km road journey because of a river and the location of the nearest bridge. Network analysis can account for the available road connections, whereas a simple distance buffer does not.

Terrain analysis

A Digital Elevation Model (DEM) is a digital representation of surface elevation, commonly organised as a grid of elevation values.

Elevation data can be used to derive geographical characteristics such as:

  • Slope: The steepness of the terrain.
  • Aspect: The compass direction towards which a slope faces.
  • Drainage characteristics: The likely direction of surface water flow and the arrangement of drainage basins.

Terrain analysis supports watershed management, flood studies, agricultural planning and the selection of suitable locations for development.

Site suitability analysis

GIS can identify areas satisfying several conditions by combining thematic layers.

Selecting a potential public facility site

Suppose a public facility should be located within 1 km of an existing road, on gently sloping land, outside a mapped flood-prone zone and near the settlement it is intended to serve.

GIS can create a road buffer, identify gently sloping land from elevation data, exclude mapped flood-prone areas and combine the remaining suitable areas with settlement information. The result is a set of potential locations for further field assessment.

GIS provides evidence to support decisions. Its results depend on the accuracy of the input information and the suitability of the criteria chosen.

Prelims focus

  • Attribute queries select features by descriptive properties.
  • Spatial queries select features by geographical relationships.
  • Intersection retains common areas; union retains combined polygon coverage.
  • Buffer analysis identifies areas within a specified distance of features.
  • Network analysis evaluates connections and routes.
  • DEM data supports analysis of elevation, slope, aspect and drainage.

[References: NCERT, Class 12, Practical Work in Geography, Part II, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 4, Spatial Information Technology, pp. 56–60; National Remote Sensing Centre, Quick Reference Guide on GIS, Chapter 4, spatial analysis operations. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: GIS Spatial Analysis, Overlay, Buffering and Terrain

body:
Agriculture and food security

Remote sensing provides information about crop distribution, vegetation condition, cultivated area, soil moisture and changes during the growing season. Repeated images can help distinguish crop growth stages and identify areas experiencing possible agricultural stress.

Healthy vegetation generally reflects near-infrared radiation strongly. Measurements in red and near-infrared wavelengths can therefore be combined to estimate vegetation greenness.

The Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is a commonly used vegetation indicator based on red and near-infrared reflectance. Healthy green vegetation generally produces relatively high positive NDVI values.

Low vegetation greenness alone does not establish the cause of agricultural stress. Water shortage, disease, nutrient deficiency, seasonal conditions and other factors may produce similar observations. Field information is necessary for reliable diagnosis.

GIS can combine crop information with rainfall, irrigation availability, soil characteristics and administrative boundaries. GNSS can provide location information for field observations and precision agriculture.

Forests and environmental monitoring

Satellite imagery helps identify forest cover, changes in vegetation extent, forest fragmentation, burned areas and the expansion of settlements into natural landscapes.

GIS allows forest information to be combined with protected-area boundaries, roads, water bodies and human settlements. These relationships support conservation planning and habitat assessment.

Thermal infrared observations can help identify unusually hot areas associated with active fires. Visible and infrared imagery acquired after a fire can help identify its geographical extent.

Water resources and oceans

Remote sensing can be used to monitor the surface extent of rivers, lakes, reservoirs, wetlands and seasonal inundation. Water generally absorbs near-infrared radiation strongly, making it distinguishable from many surrounding land surfaces.

Ocean colour sensors measure variations in reflected visible radiation from water. These measurements can be used to estimate concentrations of substances such as chlorophyll associated with phytoplankton.

Phytoplankton are microscopic photosynthetic organisms that form an important part of aquatic food chains. Satellite-derived chlorophyll information helps study marine productivity.

Thermal infrared sensors can estimate sea-surface temperature, while microwave instruments provide useful information about ocean conditions. These observations support oceanographic research, fisheries advisories and environmental monitoring.

Weather and climate studies

Meteorological satellites monitor cloud formation, atmospheric moisture, storm development and other atmospheric conditions. Frequent observations from geostationary satellites are particularly useful for tracking cyclones.

Satellite measurements also help estimate land-surface temperature, sea-surface temperature, snow cover and atmospheric constituents. Repeated observations over long periods support the study of climatic changes.

Land-surface temperature refers to the temperature of the observed surface, such as soil, roofs or vegetation. It is not necessarily equal to the air temperature measured above that surface.

Disaster management

DisasterRemote sensing informationGIS application
FloodExtent of inundationIdentify affected villages and roads
CycloneCloud systems and storm developmentAssess exposed settlements and infrastructure
DroughtVegetation and moisture indicatorsIdentify potentially affected agricultural regions
Forest fireThermal anomalies and burned areasMap affected forests and nearby settlements
LandslideVisible surface changesCombine terrain, geology and rainfall information

Microwave radar is particularly useful for flood observations when clouds obstruct conventional optical imagery. GIS can then combine the observed flood extent with settlement, road and population data to support rescue and relief planning.

Urban and regional planning

Remote sensing provides information about built-up areas, urban expansion, open spaces and changes in land cover. GIS combines this information with transport networks, population, administrative boundaries and public infrastructure.

Such integration supports assessment of urban growth, accessibility to services, infrastructure requirements and the distribution of public facilities.

Direct measurements and derived information

Remote sensing instruments measure radiation. Geographical properties such as vegetation condition, soil moisture, chlorophyll concentration and surface temperature are inferred from those measurements using appropriate methods and reference information.

Some satellite instruments can detect atmospheric gases, including methane. However, attributing an observed gas concentration to a specific activity, such as rice cultivation, and estimating its emissions may require additional geographical, atmospheric and ground-based information.

Prelims focus

  • NDVI uses red and near-infrared reflectance to indicate vegetation greenness.
  • Ocean colour observations help estimate chlorophyll concentration.
  • Thermal infrared observations support surface temperature and fire monitoring.
  • Microwave radar is useful for flood mapping under cloud cover.
  • GIS combines hazard information with geographical exposure data.
  • Trap: Satellite-derived land-surface temperature is not necessarily the same as air temperature.

[References: NCERT, Class 11, Practical Work in Geography, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 6, Introduction to Remote Sensing, pp. 75–89; NCERT, Class 12, Practical Work in Geography, Part II, 2024–25 edition, Chapter 4, Spatial Information Technology, pp. 56–64; ISRO, Earth Observation Applications; NASA Earth Observatory, Remote Sensing; NASA Applied Remote Sensing Training, Fundamentals of Remote Sensing, 2023. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
